additions.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 10: Data and data governance
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.locator: Art. 10(1)-(4) and (6); para 5 shown as deleted
additions.quote: shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose
additions.why: The one binding rule that states the criterion's standard almost word for word, and applies to all training, validation and testing data for high-risk systems, not only personal data. Para 2 lists the governance practices expected (origin of data, preparation, assumptions, bias examination, gaps). The first-pass log found this page unreliable; it now states the consolidation date and marks paragraphs 1 and 6 AMENDED and paragraph 5 DELETED. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidation as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal; EUR-Lex itself returned an empty page. EU law: it reaches UK firms only where they place systems on the EU market or their output is used there. No application date is stated here because none was read on this page.

additions.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
additions.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
additions.locator: Principle 3.2 'The use of data' (a)-(c), PDF p. 21; Principle 2.3 'Policies and procedures' (data quality management procedures), PDF pp. 15-17; para 1.5
additions.quote: The model development process should demonstrate that the data used to develop the model are suitable for the intended use
additions.why: A UK regulator's expectation on data fed to models, wider than personal data: data must be suitable, representative of the customers the model is used for and free of inappropriate bias; where it is not representative the impact must be assessed and the model treated as more uncertain. Firms need written rules for data quality, accuracy and relevance. Limits: sector-specific (banks, building societies and designated investment firms); supervisory expectation, not legislation; in effect from 17 May 2024. Already cited elsewhere in the library for governance passages.

additions.title: The Government Data Quality Framework
additions.locator: 'Data quality principles' 1-2; 'The data lifecycle'; 'Data quality dimensions'
additions.quote: It is unlikely that data will be equally fit for all purposes.
additions.why: The UK public sector's own standard for data quality: principles, a lifecycle view of where quality fails (including accuracy decaying over time and missing documentation), and dimensions against which quality is measured and tracked. Supports the criterion's higher levels (measured quality, monitored over time) and the point that quality is judged against a purpose. Limits: written for government bodies, voluntary for others, published 2020 and not AI-specific.

additions.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612)
additions.locator: para 3.13, p. 36 (PDF p. 38); summary para 16, p. 10; paras 3.12-3.14
additions.quote: Access to good-quality data was identified as a barrier to implementing AI by 62% of the 87 government bodies responding to our survey.
additions.why: Audit evidence that data quality is the practical constraint on AI: most surveyed government bodies named it as a barrier, and the auditor records that fixing data quality across government 'remains slow and difficult'. Limits: central government only; a survey of bodies' own views (the report describes the position 'as at autumn 2023'); about ability to adopt AI, not about harm to individuals. Already cited elsewhere for other passages.

additions.title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
additions.publisher: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 81 (J. Buolamwini and T. Gebru)
additions.quote: is underrepresented in benchmark datasets can nonetheless be subjected to frequent targeting
additions.why: The best-known peer-reviewed evidence that unrepresentative data produces unequal results. Two standard face datasets were 79.6% and 86.2% lighter-skinned; three commercial systems misclassified darker-skinned women at error rates up to 34.7%, against at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men (abstract). It is why the criterion asks for representative data and ties data quality to fairness testing. Limits: one task (gender classification from faces), three commercial products, a test set of 1,270 people; conference paper.

additions.title: "Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work": Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI
additions.publisher: Google Research (N. Sambasivan and others; ACM SIGCHI 2021)
additions.quote: Data cascades are pervasive (92% prevalence), invisible, delayed, but often avoidable.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed interview study of 53 AI practitioners in India, East and West Africa and the United States. Poor data practice early on caused compounding problems later that were hard to see when they began; the authors report 92% prevalence. Supports treating data quality as something to be monitored with alerts, not cleaned once. Limits: abstract only read in this pass, on the authors' employer's publications page; a qualitative sample, none from the UK; the publisher's page was not opened.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. It can now be supplemented: the first pass could not rely on the Commission's copy of EU AI Act Article 10, which is now a dated consolidated text and states the 'relevant, sufficiently representative ... free of errors and complete' standard for high-risk systems. The brief makes no EU claim, and its statement that the UK duties cover personal data only still holds for the UK GDPR; the PRA's SS1/23 shows a UK sector rule that goes wider.
